ab-wheel-rollout.note: Roll-outs gave some of the highest rectus abdominis and oblique activity, along with high lat activity.

arnold-press.note: Extrapolated from shoulder press data; the rotation starts with palms in, which keeps the front delts busy.

assisted-pull-up.note: Extrapolated from the unassisted pull-up; assistance lowers the load but not the pattern.

back-extension.note: The 45 degree Roman chair worked the erectors as much as a Romanian deadlift and the hamstrings and glutes more.

back-squat.note: Deep squats grew the quads, glutes and adductors on MRI while the hamstrings did not change, so hamstrings are left out.

band-pull-apart.note: Extrapolated from reverse fly data: pulling the band apart works the rear delts and upper back together.

barbell-bench-press.note: On a flat bench all three parts of the chest work about equally hard, with the sternal (mid) chest doing the most and the front delts and triceps helping.

barbell-curl.note: A supinated grip gives the highest biceps activity; brachialis share is estimated because surface EMG cannot reach it.

barbell-row.note: The bent-over row showed high lat and thoracic erector activity plus the highest lumbar erector load of the rows tested.

barbell-shrug.note: Shrugs mainly elevate the scapula through the upper trapezius, with smaller middle trapezius and grip contributions.

bench-dip.note: Extrapolated from bar dip data: with feet supported and hands behind you, more of the work falls on the triceps.

bulgarian-split-squat.note: Compared with the back squat it asks less of the knee and is hip dominant, so the glutes take a larger share.

cable-crunch.note: Extrapolated from the floor crunch; kneeling with a cable adds load without changing which muscles flex the spine.

cable-curl.note: Underhand cable curls produced the highest biceps and brachioradialis activity of the grips tested.

cable-fly.note: Extrapolated from dumbbell fly data: a mid-height cable fly is mostly chest with a little front delt and no triceps; raising or lowering the cables shifts work.

cable-kickback.note: An isolated hip extension where the glutes do most of the work; extrapolated from glute activation review data.

cable-lateral-raise.note: Extrapolated from dumbbell lateral raise data; the cable keeps tension at the bottom but works the same muscles.

chest-supported-row.note: Extrapolated from seated row studies; chest support removes lower back work, leaving upper back, lats and arms.

chin-up.note: The underhand grip keeps lat activity the same as a pull-up but raises biceps (and chest) activity.

close-grip-bench-press.note: Extrapolated from flat bench press data: a narrower grip moves more of the work to the triceps.

close-grip-lat-pulldown.note: Narrow grips kept lat activity close to the wide grip; a little more elbow flexion shifts some work to the biceps.

crunch.note: The crunch works the rectus abdominis with modest oblique activity and little hip flexor activity.

deadlift.note: The review finds erector spinae, gluteus maximus and hamstrings among the most active muscles; quads also work hard but are not a tracked region here.

decline-bench-press.note: A decline shifts work away from the upper chest and toward the sternal (mid and lower) chest; shares follow the flat bench with that shift.

decline-dumbbell-press.note: A decline shifts work away from the upper chest and toward the sternal (mid and lower) chest; shares follow the flat bench with that shift.

decline-sit-up.note: Extrapolated from the flat sit-up, which matched the crunch for abs but used the hip flexors far more.

dips.note: Bar dips work the chest and triceps hardest, with front delts and the shoulder blade muscles stabilising.

dumbbell-bench-press.note: Chest and front delt activity match the barbell bench press, with slightly less triceps involvement.

dumbbell-curl.note: Dumbbell curls train the same elbow flexors as the barbell, with slightly lower overall activity in the study.

dumbbell-fly.note: With straight-ish arms the triceps barely work, so the fly is almost all chest with some front delt.

dumbbell-lateral-raise.note: The lateral raise works the side delts most, with rear delts and upper traps helping, especially near the top.

dumbbell-overhead-extension.note: Arms overhead stretch the long head, which grew about 1.5 times more than with pushdowns.

dumbbell-romanian-deadlift.note: Same hip hinge as the barbell RDL, so the same split applies.

ez-bar-curl.note: The EZ curl matched the straight bar for biceps and showed slightly more brachioradialis activity.

face-pull.note: Extrapolated from reverse fly and upright row data: pulling high toward the face shares the work between rear delts and upper back.

front-raise.note: The front raise works the front delts the most of any raise and the side delts and traps the least.

front-squat.note: A more upright torso shifts work toward the quads; the split is extrapolated from back squat growth data.

glute-bridge.note: A shorter-range floor version of the hip thrust with more relative hamstring help; extrapolated from hip thrust data.

goblet-squat.note: A front-loaded deep squat, extrapolated from back squat growth data with the front load adding core work.

good-morning.note: Erector activity was clearly higher than hamstring activity; glutes were not measured, so their share is an estimate.

hack-squat.note: A guided machine squat with the back supported, so quads dominate and the lower back does little; extrapolated from squat and leg press data.

hammer-curl.note: A neutral grip lowers biceps activity relative to an underhand grip; the larger brachialis share is an anatomical estimate, not measured.

hanging-leg-raise.note: Hanging knee-ups were among the top exercises for rectus abdominis and obliques, with heavy hip flexor involvement.

hip-abduction.note: Hip abduction mostly works the gluteus medius with upper glute max help; extrapolated from side-lying abduction EMG.

hip-adduction.note: The machine targets the inner thigh adductors almost entirely; based on adduction exercise EMG in soccer players.

hip-thrust.note: The hip thrust showed much higher glute and hamstring activity than the squat, with the quads still working to hold the knee.

incline-barbell-bench-press.note: A 30 to 45 degree incline shifts work toward the upper chest (clavicular head) and the front delts, while mid chest activity drops.

incline-dumbbell-curl.note: Incline curls reached biceps activity as high as standing curls while working the long head from a stretched shoulder position.

incline-dumbbell-press.note: A 30 to 45 degree incline shifts work toward the upper chest (clavicular head), and dumbbells use a little less triceps than a barbell.

kettlebell-swing.note: Swings showed high glute activity, moderate back activity and less hamstring activity.

lat-pulldown.note: An overhand pulldown activates the lats most, with mid traps and biceps contributing and grip width changing little.

leg-extension.note: An isolation lift for the quads; knee extension training grows the rectus femoris more than squats do, alongside the larger vasti.

leg-press.note: Leg press drives the quads hard with less hamstring activity than the squat; glute and adductor shares follow squat growth data.

leg-press-calf-raise.note: Knees stay straight as in the standing calf raise, so the same split is extrapolated.

lying-leg-curl.note: Nearly all hamstrings, with the gastrocnemius helping to bend the knee.

machine-chest-press.note: The machine works the mid chest as well as a flat bench but uses less upper chest and triceps.

machine-hip-thrust.note: Same movement as the barbell hip thrust on a machine, extrapolated from barbell data.

machine-lateral-raise.note: Extrapolated from dumbbell lateral raise data; the pads guide the arms out to the side.

machine-row.note: Extrapolated from the seated cable row, which has the same supported horizontal pull.

machine-shoulder-press.note: The machine works the delts less than a barbell press, especially the side delts, because the path is fixed.

nordic-curl.note: Nordic training mainly grew the semitendinosus, with the gastrocnemius assisting at the knee.

one-arm-dumbbell-row.note: Extrapolated from rowing studies; bracing on a bench removes most lower back load and the one-sided pull asks a little of the obliques.

overhead-press.note: Pressing overhead in front of the head is led by the front delts, with side delts, triceps and a little upper chest helping.

overhead-triceps-extension.note: Arms overhead stretch the long head, which grew about 1.5 times more than with pushdowns.

pallof-press.note: Evidence is a small pilot study; resisting rotation mainly loads the obliques and deep stabilisers.

pec-deck.note: Extrapolated from dumbbell fly data: the machine guides the arc, keeping the work on the chest.

pendlay-row.note: Extrapolated from the bent-over barbell row; restarting from the floor keeps the same muscles and back demand.

pike-push-up.note: Extrapolated from overhead press data: the pike angle turns a push-up into a bodyweight shoulder press.

plank.note: In a standard plank the external obliques were most active, ahead of the lower abdominal stabilisers and upper rectus abdominis.

preacher-curl.note: Preacher curls peak biceps activity early in the lift and drop off near the top; brachialis share is estimated.

pull-up.note: Lats are similar in pull-ups and chin-ups, while the overhand grip brings more lower trapezius and less biceps than a chin-up.

push-up.note: Push-ups work the same muscles as a flat bench press at a matched effort, plus the core to hold a plank.

rear-delt-fly.note: Extrapolated from reverse fly machine data: pulling the arms out to the side works the rear delts with help from the upper back.

reverse-pec-deck.note: The reverse fly machine works the rear delts and upper back; a neutral grip raised rear delt activity.

romanian-deadlift.note: The RDL shows high hamstring activity and lower erector activity than the hamstrings.

seated-cable-row.note: Close grips favour the lats while wider, elbows-out grips shift work to the mid traps and rear delts.

seated-calf-raise.note: Bent knees take the gastrocnemius out of the movement, so the soleus does most of the work.

seated-dumbbell-press.note: Extrapolated from barbell shoulder press data; dumbbells let the elbows flare a little, which adds some side delt.

seated-leg-curl.note: Training the hamstrings at a longer length grew them more than the lying curl; the calves help only a little.

side-plank.note: The side hold recruits many trunk muscles, with the obliques working hardest and fatiguing fastest.

single-leg-calf-raise.note: A straight-knee calf raise on one leg, extrapolated from the standing calf raise study.

skull-crusher.note: Extrapolated from overhead and pushdown data: arms halfway up put the long head between the two.

smith-machine-bench-press.note: Chest and front delt activity on the Smith machine matched the free barbell bench press.

standing-calf-raise.note: With straight knees the gastrocnemius grew far more than the soleus.

step-up.note: Step-ups produced some of the highest glute activation in the review while the quads drive the knee.

stiff-leg-deadlift.note: With straighter knees the hamstrings work hard and the erectors showed the highest activation in the studies reviewed.

straight-arm-pulldown.note: Lats were most active in the straight-arm pulldown; the triceps long head also works but is not a tracked region.

sumo-deadlift.note: The wide stance raised quad activity compared with the conventional deadlift, with similar back and hamstring activity.

t-bar-row.note: Extrapolated from the bent-over barbell row; the hinged position still loads the lower back, a bit less with a close grip.

triceps-bar-pushdown.note: With the arms at your sides the long head is shortened, so pushdowns grow it less than overhead work.

triceps-rope-pushdown.note: With the arms at your sides the long head is shortened, so pushdowns grow it less than overhead work.

upright-row.note: The upright row works the side delts and traps together; a wider grip raises both.

walking-lunge.note: Forward lunges show high quad and glute activity with some hamstring involvement.

weighted-dips.note: Same pattern as bodyweight dips; added load raises effort but not the split.

weighted-pull-up.note: Same movement as the pull-up with added load, so the same split applies.

kelso-shrug.note: Not measured as such: an estimate from what pulling the shoulder blades back works (middle and lower trapezius, rhomboids). The chest support and straight arms leave the lats and biceps little to do.

keenan-flap.note: Not measured as such: estimated from the straight-arm pulldown, the closest studied exercise. Pulling the arm down to the side is the lats’ main job; the teres major helps.

behind-the-neck-press.note: Compared with pressing in front, pressing from behind the head works the front delts and chest less and the rear delts, upper traps and triceps more.

brachioradialis-curl.note: Turning the palms down takes work off the biceps and onto the brachioradialis and brachialis; the shares are an estimate from grip-position studies.

dumbbell-stiff-leg-deadlift.note: The same movement as the barbell stiff-leg deadlift with the load in the hands: hamstrings and spinal erectors work hardest, the glutes help.

box-squat.note: Sitting briefly on a box changed muscle activity very little compared with a back squat to the same depth, so the shares follow the squat.

one-arm-cable-triceps-extension.note: The same muscles as the two-arm pushdown, one arm at a time; taken overhead, the long head works at a longer length and grows more.

one-arm-machine-lateral-raise.note: The same muscles as the two-arm machine raise, one side at a time.

single-leg-extension.note: The same muscles as the two-leg extension, one leg at a time.

one-arm-pec-deck.note: The same muscles as the two-arm pec deck, one side at a time.

single-leg-press.note: Estimated from the two-leg press; on one leg the glutes also work to keep the hip steady.

single-leg-curl.note: The same muscles as the two-leg curl, one leg at a time.

one-arm-lat-pulldown.note: Estimated from the two-arm pulldown, one arm at a time.

one-arm-cable-row.note: Estimated from the seated cable row, one arm at a time.

one-arm-cable-curl.note: The same muscles as the two-arm cable curl, one arm at a time.

single-leg-romanian-deadlift.note: Estimated from the Romanian deadlift; balancing on one leg asks more of the glutes.
